lead: One lot, one building, and at least four separate layers of rule stacked on it. It is worth walking through because almost every question a community board gets asked involves more than one of these at once, and people routinely blame the wrong layer for the answer.

facts.d: A medium density residential district. Apartment buildings are permitted.
A commercial overlay mapped on top of the R6, allowing local retail and service uses the R6 alone would not.
Owned by the NYC Department of Citywide Administrative Services.
How PLUTO classifies what is there today. This describes the current use, it does not control what is allowed.
Exterior work needs Landmarks Preservation Commission review.
The Brooklyn Public Library pop-up branch, and the Brooklyn Community Board 6 district office.

layers.t: The library is permitted by the R6 itself
layers.b: A public library is Use Group III, community facilities. Use Group III is permitted as of right in every Residence District, R1 through R12. That is a deliberate choice in the Zoning Resolution: schools, houses of worship, libraries and hospitals are treated as things a residential neighborhood should be able to contain, not intrusions on it. No overlay, no special permit, no discretionary approval. The library could be here if the C1-3 overlay did not exist.

layers.t: The community board office is permitted by the overlay, not the R6
layers.b: An agency office is Use Group VII, offices and laboratories. Use Group VII is not permitted as of right in a Residence District. In R districts an office is only possible by special permit, and only in narrow circumstances. What allows it here is the C1-3 overlay, which permits commercial uses including offices on this frontage. Strip the overlay and the office becomes a non-conforming use while the library stays untouched. Same building, same lot, two uses, two entirely different sources of permission.

layers.t: Housing could be added with no rezoning at all
layers.b: R6 permits Use Group II, residences, as of right, and permits all residence types including apartment buildings. Nothing about the current institutional use or the commercial overlay removes that. A residential building here would not need a zoning map change, would not need ULURP, and would not come to the community board as a land use item. The zoning already allows it. That is worth knowing, because the public conversation usually assumes the opposite: that adding housing anywhere requires a fight over a rezoning.

layers.t: Land use describes, it does not permit
layers.b: The city records this lot as public facilities and institutions. People read that as a restriction. It is not. It is a description of what occupies the lot today, derived from the building. If the building were converted to apartments tomorrow, the land use code would change to residential and the zoning would not have moved an inch. Zoning controls what may be built. Land use records what is built. Confusing the two is the single most common mistake in a land use conversation.

lpc.t: What landmarking would and would not require
lpc.intro: The site sits in the Cobble Hill Historic District. Landmark designation is a separate body of law from zoning, administered by a different agency, and it answers a different question. Zoning asks what use is allowed and how big a building may be. Landmarks asks what the building looks like and whether a proposed change is appropriate to the district. Neither overrides the other, and a project usually needs both.
would: Any visible exterior change, windows, doors, storefront, cornice, facade material, needs LPC approval before the Department of Buildings will issue a permit.
A rooftop addition or a new building on the lot needs a Certificate of Appropriateness, which is a public hearing before the full Commission.
Demolishing a contributing building in a historic district is very difficult and requires Commission approval.
Storefront signage and awnings on a landmarked frontage need LPC sign-off, separate from any zoning sign rules.
wouldnot: LPC has no authority over use. It cannot make a use legal that zoning bars, and it cannot bar a use that zoning permits. Converting this building to housing would still be as-of-right under the R6.
Change how big a building may be
Floor area, height and setback come from the Zoning Resolution. LPC reviews whether a proposed design is appropriate, not whether the floor area is permitted.
LPC jurisdiction is over the exterior, and over interiors only where an interior landmark has been separately designated.
A Certificate of Appropriateness is an LPC process, not a land use review. It does not come to the community board as a ULURP item, although the board is notified and routinely comments.
lpc.order: In practice the sequence matters. A project here would get its Certificate of Appropriateness from LPC first, then file with the Department of Buildings, which checks zoning compliance. Neither agency waives the other.

takeaway: Four layers, four different answers, four different bodies. The R6 permits the library and would permit housing. The C1-3 overlay permits the office. The land use code describes and controls nothing. Landmarks governs the appearance and nothing else. When someone asks whether something can happen at an address, the useful first question is always: which layer are we actually talking about?

gowanus.t: Gowanus is the other half of this
gowanus.b: Gowanus is the other half of this. The 2021 rezoning created the Special Gowanus Mixed Use District and mapped much of the canal corridor as paired MX districts, written as M1-4/R6A and similar. A paired district is not manufacturing with an exception, and it is not residential with an exception. Both sets of rules run on the same lot, which is how an area can permit apartments and light manufacturing at once. That pairing is the mechanism, and it took a full ULURP action with a community board hearing and vote to put it there. It is the clearest local illustration of the distinction this page keeps drawing: changing what a lot may be used for within the rules is administrative, but changing the rules themselves is a rezoning.
